questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I speak a bit of german, and thought it would be fun to become semi fluent

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It has been the most amazing time. I don't think you can understand how much we europeans truely have in common, untill you live and breath the community.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit tricky, but the staff at the uni were very sweet and well-meaning.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Mostly guidance from the incommings team around the bureacracy of it all. A lecturers also helped secure me a spot on course which would otherwise be unavaliable to me due to my study background, which was nice of her. In that instance the usual pathways were less helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The buddy program didn't work that well for me, since the person assigned didn't have any time, but I think I was just unlucky.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was pretty hard. Comunicating in german, if you can, is helpful, and start early! If you're relentless it'll pay off in the end. And stay away from the Burschenshafts (frats). They are cult like. At least be aware, that you are in for an experience if you end up living in one. If it's a Burschenshaft that 'fences' (greman: Fechten), stay away! That's some nazi coded stuff. 

The christian dorms are generally okay. People are nice and normal, just religious. 

Consider applying to the MöFa dorm. It's a school with a connected dorm, where is easier to find space. It's exspensive, but considering that three meals a day were included when I lived there, I'd say it's worth it. You also live with germans, which helped me learn the language, after a lot of dinners where I didn't understand a word they were saying. If it wasn't for me living there, I don't think my german would have improved at all.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you live further away from the city, try to find something close to an U-bahn. They run at night more often. The S-bahn is shite. Ehrenfeld is in my oppinion the nicest area to live in, since it has a life of it's own.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very german. They were pretty acommedating to me missing a few deadlines, but god knows a few hoops have to be hopped. Ask the incommings team for help, and don't hesitate to call them. They are nice and helpful.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I think it cut three years off my life expectancy.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The incommings team is worth gold

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: This is perhaps the biggest tension point. For political science, they have very limited classes. They also comfirm your space very late in the process of registration. If you have a lot of requirements regarding the classes to take in exchange, and you study politics on the bachelor level, I'd recommend another uni. I did not end up getting the classes I needed, and have had to extend my bachelors as a consequence of that. The limited and confusing selection combined with the fact that the allocation took place so late was a major hurdle at the start of my exchange. If you are en econ or business student, I don't think you will face the same challenges, since they have a wider selection in those areas.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to ask for help.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Coming from University of Copenhagen, the political science program did not live up to the same academic standards. I think due to the german bachelor students studying social sciences in general, and not political science specifically, the courses will be a bit easy, if you are at the end of a political science bachelor.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took one MA course where the difficulty level was adjusted for me as a bachelor student. This will probably not be possiple under normal circumstances. Anyhow, if you are studying political science at KU, you will likely not ecounter anything you can't handle.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There was a bigger emphasis on presentations and generally smaller classes for political science. You had a close relationship with the lecturers, which was fun.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Authoritarian Politics
Authoritarian Legality, Agency and Administrative Law in China
Social and Welfare policy in the US
Electoral Rights - Cleavages and Trajectories
across Political Systems
Digitalization & AI: Shaping the Future of European Politics and the Way We Study It

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Take what you can as a poltical science student. There's not much to choose from. Authoritarian Politics was fun though, since the lecturer is pretty eccentric. Authoritarian Legality, Agency and Administrative Law in China was also really fun, but write to the leacturer Hannah Klöber directly if you want to take it. Otherwise they probably won't let you.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: They have a semester fee, that I put under "other", which covers amongs other things transportation. Beer is cheap though if you go to places like Soylent Green or Späti.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Beer

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There weren't many clubs, I tried to engage in some, but the wibe was weird. The sports were great though, and the intro activities for exchange students worked like a charm in helping you meet people. We made our own non-academic opportunities with the people we met in the first weeks.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of sports and some social events. Pics and Cems (I think they're called) made some fun events.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Pic's and Cems club is good, and finding some fun people in the intro week, and build a social circle around that. Expect to spend a lot of time drinking.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I mostly stayed in cologne, since I've travelled europe quite a bit. Go to Bonn at one point, and maybe use the fact a lot of cool places are only a train ride away.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Germans and danes are not that different. Learn the language though.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Learn german, and accept that you will struggle in the start. Also be insistend. The german is by nature anti social. It is our job to break open their shell. Talking to the people in your classes help, they are too polite to refuse.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: the Germans take to easily on cancelling plans. Or the classic: "I am tired, I go home now".

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Carneval is really fun.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Find housing early, force yourself to be social with new people (not too many visits and phone calls from friends) and become a regular the the metronom - wonderful jazz bar.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try to find housing south of the river, it's nicer.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Deutsch sprechen

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Learning to speak german. Also finding housing,

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Schrotty is a good club, Soylent Green is a great bar, and the germans are fun when you get to know them.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
